the bath is probably of no importance. Anyone may have had a bath. Mrs. Redfern before she went to play tennis, Captain Marshall, Miss Darnley. As I say, anyone. There is nothing in that.

Ive been checking up with Heald on this typewriting business. Not a doubt of it, it couldnt be done under an hour. Longer, if you had to stop and think here and there. That seems to me pretty well to settle it. And look at this letter.

The chambermaid heard him typing up till five minutes to eleven. Miss Darnley saw him at twenty minutes past, and the woman was dead at a quarter to twelve. He says he spent that hour typing in his room, and it seems quite clear that he was typing in his room. That washes Captain Marshall right out.
I was wondering why Miss Darnley suddenly volunteered this extra evidence.

Look here, sir, lets look at it this way. Supposing Miss Darnley wasnt on Sunny Ledge this morning as she says. That storys a lie. Now suppose that after telling us her story, she finds that somebody saw her somewhere else or alternatively that someone went to the Ledge and didnt find her there. Then she thinks up this story quick and comes and tells it to us to account for her absence. Youll notice that she was careful to say Captain Marshall didnt see her when she looked into his room.
Are you suggesting that Miss Darnleys mixed up in this? Nonsense, seems absurd to me. Why should she be?
We might take Redfern with us. He told us about it. What about you, M.
Me, I am like Miss Brewster and Mrs. Redfern, I do not like to descend perpendicular ladders.
All along—ever since I arrived here—I have been conscious—very conscious—of the forces of evil close at hand.
You remember, M. Our conversation some days ago? About the reality of evil?

I heard nothing. All I can tell you is this: that I knew instinctively as soon as I saw her that Arlena Marshall was a focus of evil. She was Evil! Evil personified! Woman can be mans help and inspiration in life—she can also be mans downfall. She can drag a man down to the level of the beast. The dead woman was just such a woman. She appealed to everything base in a mans nature. She was a woman such as Jezebel and Aholibah. Now—she has been struck down in the middle of her wickedness!
Not struck down—strangled! Strangled, Mr. Lane, by a pair of human hands.
It is the simple truth. Have you any idea, Mr. Lane, whose hands those were?
Accompany me there in a boat, Mr. Lane. We start immediately.
You also smoke a pipe, do you not, Mr. Lane?
Yes. Oh yes. My pipe is an old friend and companion.
Air quite fresh, not fishy or seaweedy, but of course this place is well above high water mark.
If theres anything up there it would have to be deliberately put there. Still, wed better have a look.
You are, I think, the tallest of us, Monsieur. Could we venture to ask you to make sure there is nothing resting on that ledge?
If by any chance theres a dope gang mixed up in this, it opens up several possibilities. First of all, the dead woman may have been in with the gang herself. Think thats likely?
I should doubt that. No, I do not think she took drugs.
Not at all. Never said anything of the sort. Just letting you know that hes the sort of fellow who could go berserk on occasions.
Mr. Blatt, there is reason to believe that Mrs. Marshall went this morning to Pixy Cove to meet someone. Have you any idea who that someone might be?
What do you think of him? Youve seen more of him than I have.

There are many of your English idioms that describe him. The rough diamond! The self-made man! The social climber! He is, as you choose to look at it, pathetic, ludicrous, blatant! It is a matter of opinion. But I think, too, that he is something else.
As a matter of fact she is wrong. I did see her, though she may not be aware of the fact. I saw her in the mirror.
Seemed to be sitting in the Chief Constables pocket all right the other day.
Thats clever of you. Its quite true, now I remember… I was, just faintly, surprised when Linda said she had been bathing.
Oh yes, I do. The string broke. It was loosely done up in the way they do in the village. It was candles—they were scattered on the floor. I helped her to pick them up.
On the contrary, Madame, there was a bedside electric lamp in perfect order.
What was her manner—when the string broke and the candles fell out of the parcel?
What are you hinting at, M. What is the meaning of all this?
It fits, Madame, here. It is part of the cat.
It is a little like your puzzle, Madame. One assembles the pieces. It is like a mosaic—many colours and patterns—and every strange-shaped little piece must be fitted into its own place.
It is one little question that I would like to ask you.
My God, Im sick of answering questions. Ive answered the police questions. I dont feel called upon to answer yours.
Mine is a very simple one. Only this. On the morning of your wifes death, did you have a bath after you finished typing and before you went out to play tennis?
A bath? No, of course I didnt! Id had a bathe only an hour earlier!
Seemed kind of indeterminate to me. Your police, I gather, have got something up their sleeves.
I shall be glad to get Mrs. Gardener away. Shes a very, very sensitive woman, and this affair has got on her nerves. Shes very highly strung.
Will you permit me, Mr. Gardener, to ask you one question?
Why, certainly, M. Delighted to assist in any way I can.
You are a man of the world—a man, I think, of considerable acumen. What, frankly, was your opinion of the late Mrs. Marshall?
But if you ask me Ill tell you my candid opinion and that is that that woman was pretty much of a darned fool!
You are very intelligent, Mademoiselle. I have thought so ever since I arrived here. It would be a pleasure to discuss this business with you.
Yes. He probably hid in that cave until he got his chance.
Would she go there to meet such a man as you describe? No, she would laugh and not go.
She maynt have known she was going to meet him. He may have sent her a message in some other persons name.
But you forget one thing, Mademoiselle. A man bent on murder could not risk coming in broad daylight across the causeway and past the hotel. Someone might have seen him.

Yes. The day of the murder was a glorious day, but the day before, remember, there was rain and thick mist. Anyone could come on to the island then without being seen. He had only to go down to the beach and spend the night in the cave. That mist, M.
You know, there is a good deal in what you have just said.
Thats my theory, for what it is worth. Now tell me yours.

Eh bien, Mademoiselle. I am a very simple person. I always incline to the belief that the most likely person committed the crime. At the very beginning it seemed to me that one person was very clearly indicated.
But you see, there is what you call a snag in the way! It seems that it was impossible for that person to have committed the crime.
Well, what do we do about it? That is my problem.
So did the late Mrs. Marshall. It is chic, eh? And very expensive?

You sat here where we are now, Mademoiselle, on the morning of the crime. You were seen here, or at least your sunshade was seen by Miss Brewster and Mr. Redfern as they passed on the sea. During the morning, Mademoiselle, are you sure you did not happen to go down to Pixy Cove and enter the cave there—the famous Pixys Cave?
On the day of the crime, Mademoiselle, somebody had been in that cave who used Gabrielle No 8.
Except for the time when you went into the hotel to Captain Marshalls room.
And you were wrong, Mademoiselle, when you thought that Captain Marshall did not see you.
He saw you, Mademoiselle, in the mirror that hangs over the table.
What are you looking at my hands for? Do you think—do you think—?
The other day you told the Chief Constable that you were fond of your stepmother and that she was kind to you.
She may not have been actively unkind—that I will grant. But you were not fond of her—Oh no—I think you disliked her very much. That was very plain to see.
Perhaps I didnt like her very much. But one cant say that when a person is dead. It wouldnt be decent.
When a person has been murdered, it is more important to be truthful than to be decent.
I would say it and I do say it. It is my business, you see, to find out who killed Arlena Marshall.
No, I do not think it was quite like that.
Will you trust me, my child, to do the best I can for you in your bitter trouble?
I havent any trouble. There is nothing you can do for me. I dont know what you are talking about.
One cant be too careful. Dont want to be overheard.
I dont mind telling you, M.

I thought you might be. Alice Corrigan was found strangled in Caesars Grove on Blackridge Heath—not ten miles from Marley Copse where Nellie Parsons was found—and both those places are within twelve miles of Whiteridge where Mr. Lane was vicar.

The Surrey police didnt at first connect her death with that of Nellie Parsons. Thats because theyd pitched on the husband as the guilty party. Dont quite know why except that he was a bit of what the Press calls a mystery man—not much known about him—who he was or where he came from. Shed married him against her peoples wishes, shed a bit of money of her own—and shed insured her life in his favour—all that was enough to raise suspicion, as I think youll agree, sir?
—so difficult to know which pieces are part of the fur rug and which are the cats tail.
I apologize. I was following a train of thought of my own.
Your mind works a funny way, doesnt it, sir? But I dare say it comes out all right in the end. If youll excuse me asking, what put you on to asking about strangulation cases in general?
You have a word in your language—slick. This crime seemed to me a very slick crime! It made me wonder if, perhaps, it was not a first attempt.
I said to myself, let us examine past crimes of a similar kind and if there is a crime that closely resembles this one—eh bien, we shall have there a very valuable clue.
No, sir, I cant say that I do really. Unless its that in each case the husband has got a cast-iron alibi.
Glad to see you. Come in. Just the man I want.
Ive decided, more or less, on a course of action. But Id like your opinion on it before I act decisively.

Ive decided to call in Scotland Yard and hand the case over to them. In my opinion, although there have been grounds for suspicion against one or two people, the whole case hinges on dope smuggling. It seems clear to me that that place, Pixys Cave, was a definite rendezvous for the stuff.
Good man. And Im pretty certain who our dope smuggler is. Horace Blatt.

It seems the most probable solution. Of course its possible that Arlena might have got on to the truth earlier, said something to Blatt about it, and some other member of the gang fixed a fake appointment with her and did her in. As I say, I think the best course is to hand the case over to Scotland Yard. Theyve a far better chance than we have of proving Blatts connection with the gang.
If I have, I am not sure that I can prove it.
What do you feel ought to be done about it?

It sounds to you, does it not, very outrageous? But indeed it seems to me a most admirable idea. We need something of the every day, the usual, to restore life to the normal. I am most anxious to see something of Dartmoor, the weather is good. It will—how shall I say, it will cheer everybody up! So aid me in this matter. Persuade everyone.
Lindas not coming. She says shes got a frightful headache.
But it will do her good to come. Persuade her, Mademoiselle.
No, no, you must come, Madame. With a headache one is better alone. Come, let us start.
And theres Mr. Blatt giving round copies to everybody without so much as asking first. He gave one to you, M.
Get a doctor—as quick as you possibly can. But Im afraid—very much afraid—it may be too late.
I dont believe it. I dont believe Linda killed her. Surely its impossible—on the evidence!
But I was with her, M. I was with her up to a quarter to twelve. I told the police so.

Your evidence gave her an alibi—yes. But what was your evidence based on? It was based on Linda Marshalls own wristwatch. You do not know of your own knowledge that it was a quarter to twelve when you left her—you only know that she told you so. You said yourself the time seemed to have gone very fast.
I am sorry to ask you this, but will you tell just what you were thinking about during that walk?
I suppose—if it is necessary… I was considering the question of—of leaving here. Just going away without telling my husband. I—I was very unhappy just then, you see.

Exactly. You were concerned over taking a step of some importance. You were, I should say, deaf and blind to your surroundings. You probably walked very slowly and occasionally stopped for some minutes whilst you puzzled things out.

How clever you are. It was just like that. I woke up from a kind of dream just outside the hotel and hurried in thinking I should be very late, but when I saw the clock in the lounge I realized I had plenty of time.

And Ill tell you this, M. Ruth—my wife—was innocent. That I know with complete and absolute certainty. In the intimacy of our life I could not have been deceived. She was an innocent victim of circumstances.
And I dont believe that Linda killed Arlena. Its ridiculous—absurd!
Do you believe that letter, then, to be a forgery?

Then if she wrote it, there are only two explanations. Either she wrote it in all good faith, knowing herself to be the murderess or—or, I say—she wrote it deliberately to shield someone else, someone whom she feared was suspected.

No, I think that idea is absurd. Linda may have realized that I was regarded with suspicion at first. But she knew definitely by now that that was over and done with—that the police had accepted my alibi and turned their attention elsewhere.
And supposing that it was not so much that she thought that you were suspected as that she knew you were guilty.

I wonder. There are, you know, several possibilities about Mrs. Marshalls death. There is the theory that she was being blackmailed, that she went that morning to meet the blackmailer and that the blackmailer killed her. There is the theory that Pixy Cove and Cave were being used for drug running, and that she was killed because she accidentally learned something about that. There is a third possibility—that she was killed by a religious maniac. And there is a fourth possibility—you stood to gain a lot of money by your wifes death, Captain Marshall?

I mean that this is not a crime that was committed single-handed. Two people were in it. It is quite true that you could not have typed that letter and at the same time gone to the cove—but there would have been time for you to have jotted down that letter in shorthand—and for someone else to have typed it in your room while you yourself were absent on your murderous errand.

You were very obviously upset and surprised by her nonappearance. Almost too obviously, perhaps. It is my theory, Mr. Redfern, that she went to Pixy Cove to meet you, and that she did meet you, and that you killed her there as you had planned to do.
Is it daft you are? I was with you on the beach until I went round in the boat with Miss Brewster and found her dead.

You killed her after Miss Brewster had gone off in the boat to fetch the police. Arlena Marshall was not dead when you got to the beach. She was waiting hidden in the cave until the coast could be clear.

You will be interested to hear that both you and your wife Christine were easily recognized and picked out by the Surrey police from a group of people photographed here. They identified you both at once as Edward Corrigan and Christine Deverill, the young woman who found the body.
Yes, you make one see it all. But thats the story from the other side. You havent told us how you came to get at the truth?
Oh, poor child, poor child. And I thought—I imagined—something quite different—that she knew something which would—

I know what it was you thought. Actually your manner frightened Linda still further. She believed that her action had really brought about Arlenas death and that you knew it. Christine Redfern worked on her too, introducing the idea of the sleeping tablets to her mind, showing her the way to a speedy and painless expiation of her crime. You see, once Captain Marshall was proved to have an alibi, it was vital for a new suspect to be found. Neither she nor her husband knew about the dope smuggling. They fixed on Linda to be the scapegoat.

Its just been too wonderful—hearing just exactly how you got your results. Its every bit as fascinating as a lecture on criminology—in fact it is a lecture on criminology. And to think my magenta wool and that sunbathing conversation actually had something to do with it? That really makes me too excited for words, and Im sure Mr. Gardener feels the same, dont you, Odell?
Mr. Gardener too was of assistance to me. I wanted the opinion of a sensible man about Mrs. Marshall. I asked Mr. Gardener what he thought of her.
Thats the kind of thing men always say to their wives,
Of course Im glad I didnt die after all. But you know, M. I meant to.
How did you know? Thats just how I did feel.
Then do not repeat to yourself the imbecilities. Just make up your mind not to hate your next stepmother.
